Lessons.Title: One of These Things Is Not Like the Others
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Compare flavors, mixtures or shapes by proportional reasoning, making defensible claims even when there is no single exact answer. First-party teaching associated with OUR/IM 2017–2019: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/2/1/preparation.html. Examples below are original Edulytiks problems and do not reproduce the publisher's artwork or protected assessment.
This exploratory lesson uses ratios and unit rates to discuss what looks or tastes similar. Multiple explanations can be valid; evaluate the reasoning and stated assumptions.

The actual publisher student lesson combines invented labels for double number lines, comparisons of three mystery mixtures, and scale-factor reasoning for crescent-shaped figures. The inventor must justify context/units and geometric matching, which a unit-rate-only score cannot assess. Student source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/students/2/2/1/index.html.

KeyConcepts.Title: Ratio of ingredients
KeyConcepts.Definition: A ratio compares the quantities in a mixture.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Two mixtures have equal concentration when their ingredient ratios match.
KeyConcepts.Example: 2 scoops per 5 cups and 4 scoops per 10 cups have the same ratio.

KeyConcepts.Title: Unit rate
KeyConcepts.Definition: A comparable intensity can be expressed per one unit.
KeyConcepts.Example: 6 scoops in 12 cups gives 0.5 scoops per cup.

KeyConcepts.Title: Evidence and assumptions
KeyConcepts.Definition: Appearance alone need not prove equivalent ratios.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Explain how measurements support or limit a claim.
KeyConcepts.Example: Unknown quantities permit reasonable hypotheses but not certainty.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare two recipes
WorkedExamples.Question: Mix A has 2 scoops of powder per 5 cups of water; B has 4 per 10. Would their concentration be equal?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
Steps: Compare the ratios and state the equal-mixture assumption.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Yes, they have equal powder-per-water ratios if the materials are the same.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both have 0.4 scoops per cup.

WorkedExamples.Title: Different concentration
WorkedExamples.Question: Mix A has 3 scoops per 6 cups; mix B has 5 scoops per 8 cups. Which has more powder per cup?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Mix B has a higher powder-to-water ratio.
WorkedExamples.Check: The comparison is per one cup of water.

WorkedExamples.Title: Open visual argument
WorkedExamples.Question: Two untitled rectangles look different sizes, but their measurements are hidden. Can appearance prove that their side ratios match?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
Steps: Identify that length and width measurements are missing.
Explain that similar appearance is not numerical evidence.
Propose measuring matching sides to compare their ratios.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No definite conclusion; measure and compare matching length ratios.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher review checks justification, not one numeric response.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare scaled geometric copies using equivalent ratios
WorkedExamples.Question: Rectangle A is 3 units wide and 5 units high. Rectangle B is 6 units wide and 10 units high, while C is 6 units wide and 8 units high. Which is a scaled copy of A?
WorkedExamples.Method: Compare both corresponding side ratios and justify whether one constant relates the two rectangles.
Steps: For B, width ratio=6/3=2 and height ratio=10/5=2.
For C, width ratio=6/3=2 but height ratio=8/5=1.6.
Both corresponding ratios agree only for B; explain why C is distorted.
WorkedExamples.Answer: B is a factor-2 scaled copy of A; C is not a scaled copy of A.
WorkedExamples.Check: The teacher reviews diagrams or ratio-table explanations; a one-number answer alone does not establish the source's representation goal.

WorkedExamples.Title: Invent a contextual double number line with units
WorkedExamples.Question: Top ticks read 0,2,4,6,8,10 and bottom ticks read 0,1,2,3,4,5. Draw them together and invent an everyday interpretation for both sets of values. Why do 10 and 5 correspond?
WorkedExamples.Method: Label both axes with chosen quantities and units, match aligned ticks and defend the chosen context to a teacher.
Steps: Invent a reasonable context: top is kilograms of apples, bottom is price in dollars.
State that each 2 kg costs $1, or $0.50 for each kg.
Check that 10 kg costs $5, and align all five nonzero tick pairs.
Ask a peer to propose a different sensible context for the same numbers.
WorkedExamples.Answer: An example is mass in kilograms versus price in dollars at $0.50/kg; other unit-consistent contexts also qualify.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks the actual double number line, context, labels and proportional argument.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Equating equal total volume with equal flavor
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Concentration depends on ingredient ratios, not only total volume.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compute ingredients per one unit of the other quantity.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating an open comparison as a unique-answer calculation
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original activity intentionally allows more than one defensible approach.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Record assumptions and evaluate explanations with a teacher rubric.

SummaryPoints: Compare flavors, mixtures or shapes by proportional reasoning, making defensible claims even when there is no single exact answer.
Divide both ingredients consistently.
Explain how measurements support or limit a claim.
Equivalent ratios can justify scaled copies of geometric figures as well as mixtures.

Visuals.Title: Powder per cup comparison
Visuals.Description: Recipe A and recipe B have equal powder-to-water rates. This first-party text table has labeled row headers so its numerical evidence is accessible without color or an image.

Visuals.Title: Double number line for a consistent illustrative unit rate
Visuals.Description: Aligned values model a hypothetical apple price of $0.50 per kilogram. Top ticks are mass in kg and bottom ticks are cost in dollars. Physical scale, labeling and invented-context justification require student work.

Lessons.Title: Introducing Proportional Relationships with Tables
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Identify constant quotients in tables and express a relationship as y=kx, including inverse constants. First-party teaching associated with OUR/IM 2017–2019: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/2/2/preparation.html. Examples below are original Edulytiks problems and do not reproduce the publisher's artwork or protected assessment.
A proportional table shows equivalent ratios in each row. When axes or designated dependent quantities are swapped, the constant becomes reciprocal.

Publisher student source-task review (2017–2019): Notice and Wonder about data; Feeding a Crowd; Making Bread Dough; Quarters and Dimes. Student completes ratios with fractions and reverse missing values, including explaining when a table looks inconsistent. Math work must be shown, not only a yes/no classifier. Original source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/students/2/2/2/index.html. First-party mathematical models may support this activity, but authentic graph drawing, invented scenarios and collaborative reasoning need teacher assessment.

KeyConcepts.Title: Constant of proportionality
KeyConcepts.Definition: The constant k links y and x in y=kx.
KeyConcepts.Rule: For every row with x≠0, calculate y/x.

KeyConcepts.Title: Proportional table
KeyConcepts.Definition: Pairs all follow one common multiplicative rule.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check every row, not just one.

KeyConcepts.Title: Reverse relationship
KeyConcepts.Definition: Interchanging quantities changes the rate to 1/k.
KeyConcepts.Example: 6 miles per hour becomes 1/6 hour per mile.

WorkedExamples.Title: Identify table constant
WorkedExamples.Question: Pairs are (2,12),(3,18),(5,30). Are they proportional?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
WorkedExamples.Check: All three quotients agree.

WorkedExamples.Title: Complete a table
WorkedExamples.Question: A runner travels at 4 miles per hour. Find the distances after 1, 2.5 and 4 hours.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
WorkedExamples.Check: The ratio stays 4 mi/h.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reverse the rate
WorkedExamples.Question: If d=5t, with d in km and t in hours, express t as a function of d.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
Steps: Divide both sides of d=5t by 5.
WorkedExamples.Check: Substituting d=10 gives t=2.

WorkedExamples.Title: Repair a contradictory ordered-pair table
WorkedExamples.Question: An invented delivery record states 1 case yields 12 rolls, 2 cases yield 36 rolls, 5 cases yield 60 rolls and 10 cases yield 120 rolls. Is the whole table proportional? How can you identify and repair the inconsistent row?
WorkedExamples.Method: Make the source-relevant table, drawing or model, calculate, and justify the answer with labeled units. For open-ended work, a teacher checks the original artifact.
Steps: Because the second quotient differs, the given table as a whole is not proportional.
If every case has 12 rolls, 2 cases should yield 24 rolls, not 36.
Show a corrected table and explain why the one inaccurate entry cannot be ignored.
WorkedExamples.Answer: The table as given is not proportional; 2 cases should be 24 rolls for the proposed 12 rolls/case model.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher reviews identification of the anomalous row and the annotated table, not a yes/no answer only.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Comparing differences instead of ratios
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Constant addition alone does not establish proportionality.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare y/x for each nonzero x.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using the same k after swapping quantities
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The inverted rate has reciprocal units and value.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use 1/k in the reverse equation.

SummaryPoints: Identify constant quotients in tables and express a relationship as y=kx, including inverse constants.
Check every row, not just one.
If y=6x then x=y/6.

Visuals.Title: Constant quotient table
Visuals.Description: The quotient y/x equals 6 in all the shown pairs. This first-party text table has labeled row headers so its numerical evidence is accessible without color or an image.

Lessons.Title: More about Constant of Proportionality
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Interpret constants as speed or conversion factors and calculate missing measurements efficiently. First-party teaching associated with OUR/IM 2017–2019: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/2/3/preparation.html. Examples below are original Edulytiks problems and do not reproduce the publisher's artwork or protected assessment.
Rates in context have units. The constant for feet-to-inches is 12 inches per foot; the inverse has feet per inch.

Publisher student source-task review (2017–2019): Equal Measures; Centimeters and Millimeters; Pittsburgh to Phoenix. Student completes both cm→mm and mm→cm conversion tables, identifies reciprocal rates with units and distinguishes length from squared-area conversion. Original source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/students/2/2/3/index.html. First-party mathematical models may support this activity, but authentic graph drawing, invented scenarios and collaborative reasoning need teacher assessment.

KeyConcepts.Title: Conversion factor
KeyConcepts.Definition: A fixed multiplier converts one measurement unit to another.

KeyConcepts.Title: Speed as constant
KeyConcepts.Definition: For constant-speed motion, distance and time are proportional.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rate units
KeyConcepts.Definition: The units of k explain what is being compared.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Read k as units of y per unit of x.
KeyConcepts.Example: 6 metres/second means 6 metres for each second.

WorkedExamples.Title: Convert a measurement
WorkedExamples.Question: How many inches are 4.5 feet?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find travel distance
WorkedExamples.Question: A cyclist travels 14 km/h for 2.5 hours. How far?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
WorkedExamples.Check: Time and speed units give km.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find constant from a table
WorkedExamples.Question: A vehicle travels 45 km in 1.5 h and 120 km in 4 h. Find its speed.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
WorkedExamples.Check: The two rates coincide.

WorkedExamples.Title: Distinguish a length conversion from a squared-area conversion
WorkedExamples.Question: A square card has a side of 3 cm. Write its side length in millimeters and then its area in both cm² and mm². Why is multiplying square centimeters by only 10 wrong?
WorkedExamples.Method: Construct or interpret a source-aligned table, graph or rate model, calculate with correct units, and justify the context. Open representations require teacher review.
Steps: The linear unit scale is 1 cm=10 mm, so side 3 cm=30 mm.
The matching square area in millimeters is 30×30=900 mm², so 1 cm²=100 mm².
A length ratio is 10 while an area ratio is 10²; label units in both original and new sketches.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 30 mm side; 9 cm²=900 mm²; an area scale uses factor 100.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks a labeled original square, numeric conversions and squared-unit reasoning.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Ignoring the rate's units
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A number by itself may represent a different conversion direction.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Include source and target units in k.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Applying 12 backwards for inches-to-feet
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Reversing a unit conversion requires division.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Divide inches by 12 to get feet.

SummaryPoints: Interpret constants as speed or conversion factors and calculate missing measurements efficiently.
distance=speed×time.
Read k as units of y per unit of x.

Visuals.Title: Feet to inches conversion
Visuals.Description: One foot is exactly twelve inches. This first-party text table has labeled row headers so its numerical evidence is accessible without color or an image.

Lessons.Title: Proportional Relationships and Equations
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Translate proportional tables and contexts into y=kx and explain k as the unit value. First-party teaching associated with OUR/IM 2017–2019: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/2/4/preparation.html. Examples below are original Edulytiks problems and do not reproduce the publisher's artwork or protected assessment.
Every row of a proportional table satisfies one equation with no additive intercept. The unit row x=1 immediately identifies k.

Publisher student source-task review (2017–2019): Number Talk Division; Feeding a Crowd Revisited; Denver to Chicago. Student writes variable equations from tables using both rates and explains quantity units in the formula. Original source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/students/2/2/4/index.html. First-party mathematical models may support this activity, but authentic graph drawing, invented scenarios and collaborative reasoning need teacher assessment.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equation model
KeyConcepts.Definition: A proportional relationship can be written y=kx.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Multiply x by k to obtain y.

KeyConcepts.Title: One-unit row
KeyConcepts.Definition: When x=1, the output equals k.
KeyConcepts.Example: If (1,3.5) is in a proportional table, k=3.5.

KeyConcepts.Title: Testing equations
KeyConcepts.Definition: Check every given pair against the equation.

WorkedExamples.Title: Build an equation
WorkedExamples.Question: Tickets cost $6 each. Find an equation for total cost y of x tickets.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
WorkedExamples.Check: The price per ticket is constant.

WorkedExamples.Title: Read k from a table
WorkedExamples.Question: Pairs are (1,2.5),(4,10),(8,20). Find k.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
WorkedExamples.Check: All table entries satisfy y=2.5x.

WorkedExamples.Title: Fill a table
WorkedExamples.Question: For y=(3/4)x, find y when x=8 and x=12.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both points have constant k=3/4.

WorkedExamples.Title: Write a rate equation for a table without confusing the variables
WorkedExamples.Question: A train covers 45 km in 3/4 hour at constant speed. Write distance d in km as a function of time t in hours and calculate its distance at t=2.5.
WorkedExamples.Method: Construct or interpret a source-aligned table, graph or rate model, calculate with correct units, and justify the context. Open representations require teacher review.
Steps: Write d=60t with units km and h.
Make a table containing (0,0),(0.75,45),(2.5,150) to justify the origin and constant rate.
WorkedExamples.Answer: d=60t; at 2.5 h travel distance 150 km.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks formula from context, table, labeled axes and units.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Adding a fixed fee in a proportional equation
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A nonzero intercept prevents y=kx.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use y=kx only when the output is zero at input zero.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Choosing k from only one inconsistent row
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: An equation must account for all table entries.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Substitute every row.

SummaryPoints: Translate proportional tables and contexts into y=kx and explain k as the unit value.
Read the y-entry at x=1.
Substitute x and y values.

Visuals.Title: Equations and ticket cost
Visuals.Description: y=6x models a $6 price per ticket with no fixed fee. This first-party text table has labeled row headers so its numerical evidence is accessible without color or an image.

Lessons.Title: Two Equations for Each Relationship
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Represent one proportional relationship in both directions and explain reciprocal constants. First-party teaching associated with OUR/IM 2017–2019: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/2/5/preparation.html. Examples below are original Edulytiks problems and do not reproduce the publisher's artwork or protected assessment.
The equation for output per input and its reverse describe the same matching pairs, but the constants and units are reciprocal.

Publisher student source-task review (2017–2019): Missing Figures; Meters and Centimeters; Filling a Water Cooler. Student reconstructs tiling-pattern drawings and compares reciprocal flow/unit-conversion equations with their dimensional meanings. Original source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/students/2/2/5/index.html. First-party mathematical models may support this activity, but authentic graph drawing, invented scenarios and collaborative reasoning need teacher assessment.

KeyConcepts.Title: Forward equation
KeyConcepts.Definition: Use y=kx when y is proportional to x.

KeyConcepts.Title: Reverse equation
KeyConcepts.Definition: Solve x=y/k to interchange input and output.

KeyConcepts.Title: Reciprocal check
KeyConcepts.Definition: Two nonzero reciprocal constants multiply to 1.

WorkedExamples.Title: Two flow equations
WorkedExamples.Question: A tap delivers 8 litres per minute. Write equations for litres L and minutes t.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
Steps: Describe the reverse rate as 1/8 min/L.
WorkedExamples.Check: At t=3, both give L=24.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find reciprocal multiplier
WorkedExamples.Question: A measurement converts by y=(5/2)x. What is the reverse?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.

WorkedExamples.Title: Interpret both directions
WorkedExamples.Question: If 9 dollars buy 3 notebooks, describe notebooks per dollar and dollars per notebook.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.

WorkedExamples.Title: Represent a water-cooler flow equation in both directions
WorkedExamples.Question: A pump fills 24 L in 6 minutes at constant rate, with no setup delay. Write liters as a function of minutes and minutes as a function of liters. What does each constant mean?
WorkedExamples.Method: Construct or interpret a source-aligned table, graph or rate model, calculate with correct units, and justify the context. Open representations require teacher review.
Steps: Forward equation V=4t with volume V in liters and time t in minutes.
Inverse equation t=V/4, or t=0.25V min/L.
Check V=12 L requires t=3 min, and discuss why the reciprocal has different units.
WorkedExamples.Answer: V=4t, t=V/4; 4 L/min and 1/4 min/L are reciprocal rates.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks double-number-line/table labels and the direction of input and output.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Failing to invert units with the rate
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Reciprocal quantities also reverse their measurement dimensions.
CommonMistakes.Correction: State units beside each constant.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Applying k to both equations
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: That would produce a different relationship.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Rearrange algebraically to obtain 1/k.

SummaryPoints: Represent one proportional relationship in both directions and explain reciprocal constants.
Reverse constant=1/k.

Visuals.Title: Forward and reverse rates
Visuals.Description: For flow of 8 litres per minute, litres and minutes swap positions when inverting the relation. This first-party text table has labeled row headers so its numerical evidence is accessible without color or an image.

Lessons.Title: Using Equations to Solve Problems
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Form proportional equations from verbal situations without relying on a supplied table. First-party teaching associated with OUR/IM 2017–2019: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/2/6/preparation.html. Examples below are original Edulytiks problems and do not reproduce the publisher's artwork or protected assessment.
Recognize the rate, choose variables with units and solve for an unknown. A ratio table is optional scaffolding, not a compulsory step.

Publisher student source-task review (2017–2019): Quotients with Decimal Points; Concert Ticket Sales; Recycling. Student derives ticket rate or can mass and value from given quantities, writes equations and solves for unknown total or input. Original source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/students/2/2/6/index.html. First-party mathematical models may support this activity, but authentic graph drawing, invented scenarios and collaborative reasoning need teacher assessment.

KeyConcepts.Title: Context-to-equation
KeyConcepts.Definition: A fixed per-unit rate yields y=kx.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Identify what x and y measure.

KeyConcepts.Title: Missing input
KeyConcepts.Definition: Solve x=y/k when y is given.
KeyConcepts.Example: Distance 28 km at 7 km/h takes 4 h.

KeyConcepts.Title: Meaning of rate
KeyConcepts.Definition: k must be explained in the actual context.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Name both numerator and denominator units.
KeyConcepts.Example: $4 per kg means price increases $4 per kg.

WorkedExamples.Title: Write from words
WorkedExamples.Question: Fruit costs $4 per kilogram. Express total cost C for mass m.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
WorkedExamples.Check: The formula has no fixed fee.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find an input
WorkedExamples.Question: A train covers 126 km at constant 42 km/h. Find the time.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find an output
WorkedExamples.Question: A printer uses 0.8 mL of ink per page. Find ink for 25 pages.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.

WorkedExamples.Title: Recover a recycling-unit rate and an unknown quantity
WorkedExamples.Question: A school recycling event gets $5.40 for 12 kg of sorted metal under a fixed per-kilogram offer. Find the amount received for 25 kg, and the mass needed to receive $18.
WorkedExamples.Method: Construct or interpret a source-aligned table, graph or rate model, calculate with correct units, and justify the context. Open representations require teacher review.
Steps: Revenue rule R=0.45m for mass m kg.
For $18, m=18/0.45=40 kg; check inverse quantities and units.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks original input/output-rate equation, table values and unit explanation.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using a rate without deciding variables
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Unlabeled numbers may be multiplied in the wrong direction.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Define the measured quantities first.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Modeling a fixed setup fee with y=kx
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A nonzero starting cost is not directly proportional.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Test whether y=0 at x=0.

SummaryPoints: Form proportional equations from verbal situations without relying on a supplied table.
Divide by the constant.
Name both numerator and denominator units.

Visuals.Title: Rate-based problems
Visuals.Description: A $4/kg price determines any total without an additive fee. This first-party text table has labeled row headers so its numerical evidence is accessible without color or an image.

Lessons.Title: Comparing Relationships with Tables
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Use quotients and contextual reasoning to classify tables as proportional, nonproportional or insufficiently evidenced. First-party teaching associated with OUR/IM 2017–2019: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/2/7/preparation.html. Examples below are original Edulytiks problems and do not reproduce the publisher's artwork or protected assessment.
When there are too few data points or an uncertain context, distinguish evidence from certainty. Multiple matched pairs establish constant quotients for the rows, not necessarily an unobserved law.

Publisher student source-task review (2017–2019): Adjusting a Recipe; Visiting the State Park; Running Laps. Student compares same-tasting and different-tasting mixtures, a fixed-vehicle-fee model and nonconstant versus constant lap rates. Original source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/students/2/2/7/index.html. First-party mathematical models may support this activity, but authentic graph drawing, invented scenarios and collaborative reasoning need teacher assessment.

KeyConcepts.Title: Quotient test
KeyConcepts.Definition: A proportional table has constant y/x at every nonzero x.

KeyConcepts.Title: Nonproportional counterexample
KeyConcepts.Definition: Different row ratios disprove proportionality for the complete table.

KeyConcepts.Title: Insufficient information
KeyConcepts.Definition: One nonzero pair does not determine whether all future values follow the rate.
KeyConcepts.Example: From (2,6) alone, many models are possible.

WorkedExamples.Title: Confirm an observed constant
WorkedExamples.Question: Pairs (2,6),(4,12),(6,18): do these table entries follow a proportional pattern?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Yes, the observed table is consistent with y=3x.
WorkedExamples.Check: All three ratios match.

WorkedExamples.Title: Disprove a ratio
WorkedExamples.Question: Pairs (2,6) and (4,13) are given. Are the values proportional?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
WorkedExamples.Check: A common k does not fit both rows.

WorkedExamples.Title: Classify limited data
WorkedExamples.Question: A table contains only the nonzero pair (3,15). Must the entire situation be proportional?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
Steps: Note that another pair could follow or violate the rate.
Request a second measurement or the relationship rule.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Not enough information to certify the situation.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher reviews justification and what data would resolve it.

WorkedExamples.Title: Distinguish proportional running from fixed-entrance fees
WorkedExamples.Question: A park charges $6 per car plus $2 per person. Another runner circles a track in 3 minutes per lap, without breaks. For three people and four laps respectively, write the mathematical models and explain which is proportional.
WorkedExamples.Method: Construct or interpret a source-aligned table, graph or rate model, calculate with correct units, and justify the context. Open representations require teacher review.
Steps: Park cost C=6+2p gives C(3)=$12 and nonzero cost C(0)=$6, so not proportional.
Running time T=3ℓ gives T(4)=12 min, and T(0)=0.
Ratios T/ℓ=3 min/lap stay constant while C/p changes with group size.
Sketch separate tables; explain the fixed fee or unchanged lap pace explicitly.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Park costs $12 for three people (not proportional); four laps take 12 min (proportional).
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher reviews the two real-context tables and classification justification.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Checking constant differences instead of quotients
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Equal additive differences are not sufficient for proportionality.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare y/x and test zero behavior.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating one pair as a proven general law
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Many relationships pass through a single nonzero point.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Record the evidence limit.

SummaryPoints: Use quotients and contextual reasoning to classify tables as proportional, nonproportional or insufficiently evidenced.
One mismatched row is enough.
Propose more measurements or context.

Visuals.Title: Inconsistent quotients
Visuals.Description: The different y/x values show that this proposed table is not proportional. This first-party text table has labeled row headers so its numerical evidence is accessible without color or an image.

Lessons.Title: Comparing Relationships with Equations
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Distinguish proportional and nonproportional formulas and explain why y=kx characterizes proportional relationships. First-party teaching associated with OUR/IM 2017–2019: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/2/8/preparation.html. Examples below are original Edulytiks problems and do not reproduce the publisher's artwork or protected assessment.
A nonzero intercept changes the output at x=0. Algebraically equivalent forms count as proportional if they reduce to y=kx.

Publisher student source-task review (2017–2019): Patterns with Rectangles; More Conversions; Total Edge Length Surface Area and Volume. Student distinguishes proportionality in unit conversion, temperature offset and cube edge versus side, area versus side and volume versus side. Original source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/students/2/2/8/index.html. First-party mathematical models may support this activity, but authentic graph drawing, invented scenarios and collaborative reasoning need teacher assessment.

KeyConcepts.Title: Proportional form
KeyConcepts.Definition: An equation equivalent to y=kx has zero output when x=0.

KeyConcepts.Title: Nonzero intercept
KeyConcepts.Definition: An equation y=kx+b with b≠0 is not proportional.

KeyConcepts.Title: Table test
KeyConcepts.Definition: Calculate several (x,y) pairs to inspect ratios and the origin.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check x=0 and at least two nonzero x values.

WorkedExamples.Title: Simplify an equation
WorkedExamples.Question: Does 3y=12x represent a proportional relationship?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
WorkedExamples.Check: The origin satisfies the relation.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reject an intercept
WorkedExamples.Question: Does y=5x+7 represent a proportional relationship?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
WorkedExamples.Check: Proportional relationships pass through the origin.

WorkedExamples.Title: Build a diagnostic table
WorkedExamples.Question: Compare y=2x and y=2x+3 at x=0,1,2.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
WorkedExamples.Check: The second equation has intercept 3.

WorkedExamples.Title: Test degree conversion and cube formulas for proportionality
WorkedExamples.Question: Decide which relationships are proportional: Celsius C to Fahrenheit F=1.8C+32, inches n to centimeters c=2.54n, cube side s to total edge E=12s, side to area A=6s², and side to volume V=s³.
WorkedExamples.Method: Make the source-relevant table, drawing or model, calculate, and justify the answer with labeled units. For open-ended work, a teacher checks the original artifact.
Steps: The Fahrenheit conversion has an intercept 32, so F/C is not constant.
Centimeters to inches satisfy c=2.54n and the origin.
A cube has 12 equal edges so E=12s, also through the origin.
Surface area and volume involve s² or s³; comparing s=1 and s=2 disproves a constant quotient.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Only inch→cm and cube side→total edge length are proportional among these five relationships.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks the student-built numerical tables and explanation of area versus length; not every graph through two points proves a global relationship.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Rejecting 2y=6x because it is not written y=kx
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Equivalent algebraic forms may still be proportional.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Solve for y before classifying.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Calling every straight-line formula proportional
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Lines with nonzero intercepts are not proportional.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check the origin.

SummaryPoints: Distinguish proportional and nonproportional formulas and explain why y=kx characterizes proportional relationships.
Test (0,0).
Check x=0 and at least two nonzero x values.

Visuals.Title: Nonproportional intercept
Visuals.Description: The line y=5x+7 starts at 7 and does not pass through (0,0). This first-party text table has labeled row headers so its numerical evidence is accessible without color or an image.

Lessons.Title: Solving Problems about Proportional Relationships
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Ask for missing information, decide whether a proportional model is appropriate, and use an equation to solve an authentic situation. First-party teaching associated with OUR/IM 2017–2019: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/2/9/preparation.html. Examples below are original Edulytiks problems and do not reproduce the publisher's artwork or protected assessment.
Some contexts require a learner to ask questions before the rate and time are known. Info-gap reasoning is an open explanation requiring teacher review.

Publisher student source-task review (2017–2019): What Do You Want to Know?; Info Gap Biking and Rain; Moderating Comments. Student must solicit specific missing data from a partner and decide which rate is relevant before solving a quantitative case. Original source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/students/2/2/9/index.html. First-party mathematical models may support this activity, but authentic graph drawing, invented scenarios and collaborative reasoning need teacher assessment.

KeyConcepts.Title: Information gap
KeyConcepts.Definition: A problem can omit a required quantity.
KeyConcepts.Rule: List needed rate, measurement and assumptions.
KeyConcepts.Example: A travel-time calculation needs distance and speed.

KeyConcepts.Title: Model applicability
KeyConcepts.Definition: A constant rate with zero initial quantity supports y=kx.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Ask about fixed fees or variable rates.
KeyConcepts.Example: A taxi base fare breaks direct proportionality.

KeyConcepts.Title: Solve with units
KeyConcepts.Definition: Use d=vt and interpret the result.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check that distance and speed units agree.
KeyConcepts.Example: At 12 km/h for 2.5 h, distance=30 km.

WorkedExamples.Title: Identify needed data
WorkedExamples.Question: A cyclist wants to know travel time for a 36 km trip. What additional value is essential if speed is constant?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
Steps: Ask for speed v in km/h.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks whether missing information is identified and explained.

WorkedExamples.Title: Solve an info gap
WorkedExamples.Question: The cyclist travels 36 km at 12 km/h. Find the time.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
WorkedExamples.Check: 12 km/h×3 h=36 km.

WorkedExamples.Title: Disprove a poor model
WorkedExamples.Question: A taxi charges $5 plus $2 per km. Is price proportional to distance?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
Steps: A direct proportional price requires zero cost at zero distance.
WorkedExamples.Check: The fixed base fare makes the relationship nonproportional.

WorkedExamples.Title: Ask for and solve a missing distance-time detail
WorkedExamples.Question: A cyclist travels 90 km, but the time is unknown. One partner has a separate card saying the constant pace was 15 km/h. What question is required, and what travel time follows?
WorkedExamples.Method: Construct or interpret a source-aligned table, graph or rate model, calculate with correct units, and justify the context. Open representations require teacher review.
Steps: Identify that distance alone cannot determine duration.
Ask the partner for a reliable speed or time value and its units.
With speed 15 km/h, apply t=90/15=6 h.
Check 15 km/h×6 h=90 km and explain why the missing information matters.
WorkedExamples.Answer: The missing quantity is speed (or time). With 15 km/h, duration is 6 hours.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher evaluates authentic information-gap dialogue and a defensible rate assumption.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Solving without verifying a fixed rate
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Some situations are not directly proportional.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check the context and any starting amount.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Hiding an essential assumption
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A numeric result may depend on speed or cost assumptions.
CommonMistakes.Correction: State what information was requested and how it was used.

SummaryPoints: Ask for missing information, decide whether a proportional model is appropriate, and use an equation to solve an authentic situation.
Ask about fixed fees or variable rates.
Check that distance and speed units agree.

Visuals.Title: Cyclist at a fixed rate
Visuals.Description: Distance is 12 kilometres per hour; missing-information tasks must specify speed. This first-party text table has labeled row headers so its numerical evidence is accessible without color or an image.

Lessons.Title: Introducing Graphs of Proportional Relationships
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Plot points from tables and recognize proportional graphs as lines through the origin. First-party teaching associated with OUR/IM 2017–2019: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/2/10/preparation.html. Examples below are original Edulytiks problems and do not reproduce the publisher's artwork or protected assessment.
Graph values with clearly labeled axes. A proportional relationship has all points (x,kx) on the same straight line through (0,0).

Publisher student source-task review (2017–2019): Notice These Points; T-shirts for Sale; Matching Tables and Graphs. Student plots on axes, pairs tables with graphs and explains why a proportional graph passes the origin but a shifted line does not. Original source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/students/2/2/10/index.html. First-party mathematical models may support this activity, but authentic graph drawing, invented scenarios and collaborative reasoning need teacher assessment.

KeyConcepts.Title: Origin
KeyConcepts.Definition: The origin is the point (0,0).
KeyConcepts.Rule: Every directly proportional graph passes through it.

KeyConcepts.Title: Coordinate table
KeyConcepts.Definition: Each input-output pair becomes one point.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Plot x horizontally and y vertically.

KeyConcepts.Title: Nonproportional graph
KeyConcepts.Definition: A line not passing through the origin is not a direct proportion.
KeyConcepts.Example: y=3x+2 crosses the vertical axis at 2.

WorkedExamples.Title: Plot a proportional rule
WorkedExamples.Question: Generate points for y=4x at x=0,1,2.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
WorkedExamples.Check: The three points share a line through the origin.

WorkedExamples.Title: Check graph membership
WorkedExamples.Question: Does point (3,15) lie on the line y=5x?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
WorkedExamples.Check: The point satisfies the equation.

WorkedExamples.Title: Distinguish a shifted line
WorkedExamples.Question: Find the y-intercept of y=2x+6 and decide if proportional.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
WorkedExamples.Check: The graph misses the origin.

WorkedExamples.Title: Sort a through-origin rate graph from an offset graph
WorkedExamples.Question: Compare table A: (0,0),(1,6),(2,12),(3,18) with B: (0,10),(1,8),(2,6),(3,4). Plot both and explain which is proportional.
WorkedExamples.Method: Make the source-relevant table, drawing or model, calculate, and justify the answer with labeled units. For open-ended work, a teacher checks the original artifact.
Steps: Plot both sets with labeled x and y axes and equal tick spacing.
A satisfies y=6x, contains (0,0), and has a common output/input ratio 6 for x>0.
B satisfies y=10−2x and is not at the origin at x=0.
Explain that a line alone is not enough; a proportional graph must pass the origin.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Table A is proportional, k=6. Table B is not, because its y-intercept is 10.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher reviews the two plotted graphs and the origin/units explanation.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Interchanging axes without updating interpretation
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Graph coordinates have a defined x and y order.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Label both axes and each plotted coordinate.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Calling every line proportional
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A straight line is not sufficient.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Verify it passes through the origin.

SummaryPoints: Plot points from tables and recognize proportional graphs as lines through the origin.
Plot x horizontally and y vertically.
Check y at x=0.

Visuals.Title: Coordinates on a proportional line
Visuals.Description: Points for y=4x lie on a line through the origin. This first-party text table has labeled row headers so its numerical evidence is accessible without color or an image.

Lessons.Title: Interpreting Graphs of Proportional Relationships
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Read a graph's constant of proportionality, explain the meaning of (1,k), and interpret rates in context. First-party teaching associated with OUR/IM 2017–2019: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/2/11/preparation.html. Examples below are original Edulytiks problems and do not reproduce the publisher's artwork or protected assessment.
Axis labels and units are not decoration: the point (1,k) means k units of y for one unit of x.

Publisher student source-task review (2017–2019): What Could the Graph Represent?; Tyler's Walk; Seagulls Eat What?. Student chooses axis quantity/units, interprets plotted points including (1,k) and relates graphs to original contexts. Original source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/students/2/2/11/index.html. First-party mathematical models may support this activity, but authentic graph drawing, invented scenarios and collaborative reasoning need teacher assessment.

KeyConcepts.Title: Point (1,k)
KeyConcepts.Definition: The output at input 1 is the constant k.
KeyConcepts.Example: (1,8) means 8 units of y per x.

KeyConcepts.Title: Contextual slope
KeyConcepts.Definition: A steeper graph of distance over time means faster speed when axes share scales.

KeyConcepts.Title: Graph-to-equation
KeyConcepts.Definition: A point and the origin determine the rate for proportional data.

WorkedExamples.Title: Interpret a distance graph
WorkedExamples.Question: A cyclist's distance-time graph includes (1,12). Find and interpret k.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
WorkedExamples.Check: For 2 hours the graph predicts 24 km.

WorkedExamples.Title: Write an equation from a point
WorkedExamples.Question: A proportional graph passes through (0,0) and (3,18). Find its equation.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
WorkedExamples.Check: The given point fits.

WorkedExamples.Title: Interpret a second point
WorkedExamples.Question: For y=2.5x, where x is hours and y is litres, what does (4,10) mean?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
Steps: Read 4 hours on the horizontal axis.
WorkedExamples.Check: The interpretation uses both axis units.

WorkedExamples.Title: Interpret a rate and inverse rate using two graph points
WorkedExamples.Question: A water tank fills uniformly, with plotted points (t,V)=(0,0),(1.5,9),(4,24). Find the volume per hour, an inverse-time equation, and label the point (1,k).
WorkedExamples.Method: Construct or interpret a source-aligned table, graph or rate model, calculate with correct units, and justify the context. Open representations require teacher review.
Steps: The rate k=V/t=9/1.5=6 L/h, consistent with 24/4.
The proportional equation is V=6t with t in hours.
The inverse is t=V/6, representing 1/6 hour per liter.
On a labeled graph, (1,6) marks the volume after one hour; justify why this isn't a y-intercept.
WorkedExamples.Answer: k=6 L/h; V=6t and t=V/6; point (1,6) is one-hour volume.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks graphed axes/units and the meaning of the unit-rate point.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Reading (1,k) as the total for all times
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The point gives output at input one, not at every input.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Describe it as a per-unit rate.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Ignoring axis labels
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Slope units depend on which quantity is horizontal.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Interpret the axes before computing or naming k.

SummaryPoints: Read a graph's constant of proportionality, explain the meaning of (1,k), and interpret rates in context.
Calculate k=y/x.
Find k and write y=kx.

Visuals.Title: Rate from a graph
Visuals.Description: Distance-time point (1,12) indicates 12 kilometres per hour. This first-party text table has labeled row headers so its numerical evidence is accessible without color or an image.

Lessons.Title: Using Graphs to Compare Relationships
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Compare two proportional graphs on the same axes by their slopes and corresponding rates. First-party teaching associated with OUR/IM 2017–2019: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/2/12/preparation.html. Examples below are original Edulytiks problems and do not reproduce the publisher's artwork or protected assessment.
With the same labeled axes and scales, the steeper proportional graph represents a larger constant of proportionality.

Publisher student source-task review (2017–2019): Fraction Number Talk; Race to the Bumper Cars; Space Rocks and Rope. Student draws multiple labeled lines on one graph, compares speeds and interprets a delayed start that is not proportional to the same global time origin. Original source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/students/2/2/12/index.html. First-party mathematical models may support this activity, but authentic graph drawing, invented scenarios and collaborative reasoning need teacher assessment.

KeyConcepts.Title: Steepness and k
KeyConcepts.Definition: For y=kx, larger positive k gives a steeper line.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Compare rise for the same run.

KeyConcepts.Title: Same-axis comparison
KeyConcepts.Definition: Rates are comparable only when graph axes and units are consistent.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Compare at one common x value.

KeyConcepts.Title: Unlabeled scale reasoning
KeyConcepts.Definition: Even if numerical tick labels are unavailable, relative steepness can compare positive rates on identical axes.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Do not invent exact k without scale labels.
KeyConcepts.Example: The steeper distance-time line indicates faster travel.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare cyclists
WorkedExamples.Question: Cyclist A has d=12t; cyclist B has d=8t. Which is faster?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
WorkedExamples.Check: At t=2 h, A travels 24 km and B 16 km.

WorkedExamples.Title: Use two points
WorkedExamples.Question: Line A passes through (2,14), B through (2,10), both from origin. Which has greater k?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.

WorkedExamples.Title: Qualitative comparison
WorkedExamples.Question: Two proportional lines share axes and origin, but no numeric tick labels are provided. What can be concluded from their steepness?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
Steps: Assume axes share the same orientation and scale.
Compare which line rises more for the same horizontal run.
State only the rate ordering, not exact numeric rates.
WorkedExamples.Answer: The steeper positive line has the larger k; exact values are unknown.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher reviews the representation-dependent argument.

WorkedExamples.Title: Distinguish a delayed departure on a shared distance-time graph
WorkedExamples.Question: Runners A and B both finish a 50 m path in 40 seconds. A starts at t=0; B starts after 10 seconds. Assuming constant speed after each starts, determine points for each at t=20 and at t=40, and explain which distance-time graph is proportional to t measured since the common t=0.
WorkedExamples.Method: Make the source-relevant table, drawing or model, calculate, and justify the answer with labeled units. For open-ended work, a teacher checks the original artifact.
Steps: Runner A has rate 50/40=1.25 m/s, so at t=20 A is 25 m.
Runner B has 30 seconds of motion from t=10 to t=40, rate 50/30=5/3 m/s.
At t=20, runner B has traveled (20−10)×5/3=50/3≈16.67 m; at t=40 both reach 50 m.
Draw A from (0,0) to (40,50), and B from (10,0) to (40,50); B is offset in common time and not proportional to t over the full experiment.
WorkedExamples.Answer: At t=20: A=25 m, B≈16.67 m; both 50 m at t=40. Only A is proportional to the shared t from 0.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks two distinct lines, common axis labels, delayed start, and correct interpretation, not a formula alone.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Comparing lines from differently scaled graphs
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Visual steepness alone is not comparable if axes differ.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use the same axes or compute rates in common units.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Inventing a numerical slope from an unlabeled graph
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Without tick values exact k is not determined.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Limit the claim to relative steepness.

SummaryPoints: Compare two proportional graphs on the same axes by their slopes and corresponding rates.
Compare at one common x value.
Do not invent exact k without scale labels.

Visuals.Title: Compare two cyclists
Visuals.Description: Both use the same hours and kilometers, allowing a meaningful slope comparison. This first-party text table has labeled row headers so its numerical evidence is accessible without color or an image.

Lessons.Title: Two Graphs for Each Relationship
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Coordinate tables, equations and graphs after swapping axes; explain why reciprocal constants describe the same relation. First-party teaching associated with OUR/IM 2017–2019: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/2/13/preparation.html. Examples below are original Edulytiks problems and do not reproduce the publisher's artwork or protected assessment.
The point (a,b) gives k=b/a when y is vertical. Swapping axes maps it to (b,a), giving the reciprocal constant a/b.

Publisher student source-task review (2017–2019): True or False Fractions and Decimals; Tables Graphs Equations; Hot Dog Eating Contest. Student coordinates a changing table, graph point and equation and explains both direct and swapped-axis rates. Original source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/students/2/2/13/index.html. First-party mathematical models may support this activity, but authentic graph drawing, invented scenarios and collaborative reasoning need teacher assessment.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equation from a point
KeyConcepts.Definition: For a nonzero a, point (a,b) on y=kx gives k=b/a.

KeyConcepts.Title: Axis reversal
KeyConcepts.Definition: Swapping x and y converts each (a,b) to (b,a).

KeyConcepts.Title: Reciprocal slope
KeyConcepts.Definition: The inverse graph has k_inv=1/k for k≠0.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Multiply forward and inverse rates to check 1.

WorkedExamples.Title: Forward and inverse equations
WorkedExamples.Question: Distance is 4 times time: d=4t. Give equation for time as function of distance.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
WorkedExamples.Check: Rates 4 and 1/4 are reciprocal.

WorkedExamples.Title: Swap a graph point
WorkedExamples.Question: An original proportional graph has (2,8). What is the matching point after exchanging axes?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both represent the same paired values.

WorkedExamples.Title: Build two tables
WorkedExamples.Question: For y=3x, list two positive pairs and the inverse pairs.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
Steps: Check inverse y=(1/3)x in the swapped coordinates.
WorkedExamples.Check: The rates multiply to 1.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reverse a graph of the same constant-flow relationship
WorkedExamples.Question: A machine produces 18 parts in 3 minutes at constant pace. Graph parts p against minutes t, then switch axes and graph t against p. Explain the two rates.
WorkedExamples.Method: Construct or interpret a source-aligned table, graph or rate model, calculate with correct units, and justify the context. Open representations require teacher review.
Steps: First graph points include (t,p)=(0,0),(1,6),(3,18) and equation p=6t.
The inverse rate is 1/6 minute per part; compare roles of x and y labels rather than treating graph rotation as a new machine.
WorkedExamples.Answer: p=6t and t=p/6; 6 parts/min versus 1/6 min/part.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks both axes/graphs and reciprocal relationship justification.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Keeping the original k after exchanging axes
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Swapping quantities changes the y-per-x rate.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Take the reciprocal and update units.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Swapping the coordinates but not axis labels
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A graph is not interpretable without labels.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Keep the quantities and axes consistent.

SummaryPoints: Coordinate tables, equations and graphs after swapping axes; explain why reciprocal constants describe the same relation.
Change labels and formula together.
Multiply forward and inverse rates to check 1.

Visuals.Title: Swap axes to invert rate
Visuals.Description: Forward points (hours, distance) correspond to inverse points (distance, hours). This first-party text table has labeled row headers so its numerical evidence is accessible without color or an image.

Lessons.Title: Four Representations
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Evaluate equivalent tables, equations, graphs and contexts; construct and critique proportional and nonproportional examples. First-party teaching associated with OUR/IM 2017–2019: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/2/14/preparation.html. Examples below are original Edulytiks problems and do not reproduce the publisher's artwork or protected assessment.
A proportional relationship can appear in multiple consistent forms. Comparison requires checking unit rates, origin behavior and actual context.

Publisher student source-task review (2017–2019): Which is the Bluest?; One Scenario Four Representations; Make a Poster. Student invents both proportional and nonproportional situations and represents each in words, table, labeled graph and equation with reasons. Original source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/students/2/2/14/index.html. First-party mathematical models may support this activity, but authentic graph drawing, invented scenarios and collaborative reasoning need teacher assessment.

KeyConcepts.Title: Context
KeyConcepts.Definition: A repeated per-unit quantity without fixed start can be proportional.
KeyConcepts.Rule: State the quantities and constant rate.

KeyConcepts.Title: Table and equation
KeyConcepts.Definition: A table should satisfy one y=kx equation.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check quotients for every nonzero row.

KeyConcepts.Title: Graph and critique
KeyConcepts.Definition: A proportional graph passes through (0,0) and has constant slope.
KeyConcepts.Example: y=5x+2 has fixed fee and is not proportional.

WorkedExamples.Title: Match four representations
WorkedExamples.Question: A shop charges $5 per identical item. Give an equation, two table rows and graph points.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
Steps: Include the origin (0,0) on the line.
WorkedExamples.Check: All representations use $5 per item.

WorkedExamples.Title: Critique a proposed match
WorkedExamples.Question: A table is (1,5),(2,10) but a graph passes through (0,2). Can it describe y=5x?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
WorkedExamples.Check: The intercept contradicts the equation.

WorkedExamples.Title: Invent a nonproportional example
WorkedExamples.Question: Create a context and equation with a fixed cost plus $5 per unit.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Example: printing costs $3 plus $5 per page; y=3+5x.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher reviews the context and explanations; different valid examples exist.

WorkedExamples.Title: Author a proportional and nonproportional four-representation project
WorkedExamples.Question: A museum sells ordinary entry tickets for $5 each, while a different museum charges $8 per group plus $3 per visitor. Construct a six-row table, words, labeled graph and algebraic rule for each. Explain how to decide if each is proportional.
WorkedExamples.Method: Make the source-relevant table, drawing or model, calculate, and justify the answer with labeled units. For open-ended work, a teacher checks the original artifact.
Steps: Describe assumptions and quantities: visitors x and total cost y in dollars.
For first museum use y=5x; rows for x=0,1,2,3,4,5 give y=0,5,10,15,20,25.
For second museum use y=8+3x; matching y rows are 8,11,14,17,20,23.
Graph both six-row sets on separate or labeled axes, and explain that only the first is through (0,0) and has constant price/visitor.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Two original tables, labeled graphs and stories; first proportional (k=5), second nonproportional ($8 intercept).
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher-only rubric: realistic context, 6 correct pairs, axes and units, proper formulas, why proportional/nonproportional, clear student-authored poster.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating any rising graph as proportional
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The origin and constant quotient matter.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Verify all four representations agree.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Leaving out units from k
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A contextual rate needs units.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Write dollars per item, km per hour, or the actual measured ratio.

SummaryPoints: Evaluate equivalent tables, equations, graphs and contexts; construct and critique proportional and nonproportional examples.
Check quotients for every nonzero row.
Explain mismatches across representations.

Visuals.Title: Representations of unit price
Visuals.Description: A fixed $5 per item gives one consistent table, equation and graph. This first-party text table has labeled row headers so its numerical evidence is accessible without color or an image.

Lessons.Title: Using Water Efficiently
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Model water usage with realistic estimates, compare baths and showers and defend assumptions in an open-ended analysis. First-party teaching associated with OUR/IM 2017–2019: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/2/15/preparation.html. Examples below are original Edulytiks problems and do not reproduce the publisher's artwork or protected assessment.
The original investigation requires students to research or estimate quantities, explain assumptions and present a visual report. No single universal bath-or-shower answer is valid.

Publisher student source-task review (2017–2019): Comparing Baths and Showers; Saving Water; Representing Water Usage. Student researches/assumes physical flow and bath water data, defends conditions, draws a graph, writes two inverse equations and exchanges a project explanation. Original source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/students/2/2/15/index.html. First-party mathematical models may support this activity, but authentic graph drawing, invented scenarios and collaborative reasoning need teacher assessment.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rate of water flow
KeyConcepts.Definition: Water used can be modeled as flow rate times time.

KeyConcepts.Title: Break-even comparison
KeyConcepts.Definition: Find duration where modeled shower use matches a chosen bath volume.

KeyConcepts.Title: Assumptions and evidence
KeyConcepts.Definition: Different fixtures and habits change the conclusion.
KeyConcepts.Rule: State measured or estimated rates and volumes.
KeyConcepts.Example: A lower-flow shower may use less water over the same duration.

WorkedExamples.Title: Estimate a shower
WorkedExamples.Question: A shower flows at 8 L/min for 6 minutes. Estimate water used.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
WorkedExamples.Check: The model assumes constant flow.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare with a bath
WorkedExamples.Question: A bath uses 80 L; the shower flows 8 L/min. When would the shower use the same amount?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.

WorkedExamples.Title: Defend an assumption
WorkedExamples.Question: A student says 'showers always save water'. Is that proven from one 6-minute shower using 48 L and one 80 L bath?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the stated mathematical model, show each relationship explicitly and check the units or representations.
Steps: Notice flow and time could change.
Explain why a single comparison does not prove an always claim.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No. The given shower uses less water than the given bath, but other rates and durations may reverse the result.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher reviews assumptions, data sources, the model and presentation.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare baths with showers under explicit uncertain assumptions
WorkedExamples.Question: A fictional bath uses 70 liters; a shower flows 8 liters/minute. Estimate use for 5, 9 and 12 minutes, when a shower exceeds the bath, and provide inverse equations.
WorkedExamples.Method: Make the source-relevant table, drawing or model, calculate, and justify the answer with labeled units. For open-ended work, a teacher checks the original artifact.
Steps: State assumptions: full bath uses 70 L and flow remains constant at 8 L/min.
The shower model is V=8t; for 5,9,12 minutes obtain 40,72,96 L.
Solve 8t=70 to get t=8.75 minutes; longer showers exceed 70 L.
Write t=V/8 and graph the rate line from (0,0) with axes minutes and liters. Compare to the horizontal 70 L bath reference.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 5 min 40 L, 9 min 72 L, 12 min 96 L; threshold 8.75 min. Equations V=8t and t=V/8.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher reviews source/assumptions for genuine investigation, labeled graph and qualifications about bath filling or varying flow.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claiming one fixture always saves water
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Real usage depends on duration, flow rate and bath volume.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare quantitative scenarios with stated assumptions.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Auto-grading a personal research conclusion from one target number
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source asks for research and argument, not a universal numeric fact.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Require teacher review of data quality, calculation and justification.

SummaryPoints: Model water usage with realistic estimates, compare baths and showers and defend assumptions in an open-ended analysis.
